english: Let $F:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that $F'(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^{2}\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}$ for all $x>0$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=0$. Then $F(1)$ is equal to
hindi: माना कि $F:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ एक अवकलनीय फलन है जिसके लिए सभी $x>0$ के लिए $F'(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^{2}\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}$ तथा $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=0$ है। तब $F(1)$ बराबर है
solution_full: For $x>0$ put $x=\dfrac1t$ with $t>0$. Then $x^{2}+x+1=\dfrac{1+t+t^{2}}{t^{2}}$, so $\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}=\dfrac{\sqrt{t^{2}+t+1}}{t}$, and $dx=-\dfrac{dt}{t^{2}}$.
As $x\to\infty$, $t\to0^{+}$ and $F\to-1+\dfrac12\log_{e}\dfrac32+C$. This must be $0$, so $C=1-\dfrac12\log_{e}\dfrac32$.
Check: $F'>0$ and $F\to0$ at infinity, so $F(1)<0$; indeed $1-\sqrt3+\dfrac12\log_{e}(2.155)\approx-0.348$. Options (A) and (C) carry sign slips and (D) loses the factor $\dfrac12$.
originality_note: New: the antiderivative is pinned down by its limit at infinity, which after the reciprocal substitution becomes the value at t = 0, so the normalising constant contains a logarithm that partly cancels with the value at t = 1 (way 5). Closest known: textbook integrals of 1/(x^2 sqrt(ax^2+bx+c)) by x = 1/t. Different because: the evaluation is relative to infinity, which the substitution turns into an ordinary endpoint.
key_step: x = 1/t reduces the integrand to -t/sqrt(t^2+t+1), which is split into a derivative part and a standard 1/sqrt(quadratic) part.
justification: A routine chain of standard steps (reciprocal substitution, numerator splitting, standard form, two evaluations) with no hidden idea. Level 2 like 2026-P2-Q3 (L2) separable-DE chain; options allow a sign check.
